meta.subject: science
meta.description: Ecology facts: food chains, biomes, carbon cycle, nitrogen cycle, ecosystems, conservation, human impact, water cycle, population dynamics

facts.statement: A food chain shows the linear path of energy from producers to consumers to decomposers
Producers (autotrophs) make their own food through photosynthesis, forming the base of food chains
Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers; secondary consumers eat primary consumers; tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers
Decomposers (fungi and bacteria) break down dead organisms and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem
A food web is more realistic than a food chain because it shows the interconnected feeding relationships in an ecosystem
Only about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost as heat
Because energy is lost at each level, there are typically fewer organisms at higher trophic levels (energy pyramid)
An apex predator is at the top of a food chain with no natural predators (e.g., wolves, eagles, sharks)
Omnivores eat both plants and animals (e.g., bears, humans, pigs) and can occupy multiple trophic levels
Detritivores (earthworms, millipedes) physically break down dead matter, while decomposers (bacteria, fungi) chemically break it down
Biomass decreases at higher trophic levels: there is more total mass of producers than primary consumers, and so on up the chain
Photosynthesis converts solar energy into chemical energy (glucose): 6CO2 + 6H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6O2
In deep ocean ecosystems, chemosynthetic bacteria are the producers, using chemical energy from hydrothermal vents instead of sunlight
Scavengers (vultures, hyenas) feed on dead animals but do not kill them, filling an important ecological niche
All living things need energy to survive; animals get energy by eating food, while plants get energy from sunlight
A trophic cascade occurs when changes at the top of a food chain cause dramatic effects at lower levels; reintroducing wolves to Yellowstone restored river ecosystems

common_errors.wrong: removing one species from a food web only affects that species
common_errors.correct: Removing a species can have cascading effects throughout the food web, affecting populations at multiple trophic levels.

common_errors.wrong: the sun is not part of a food chain
common_errors.correct: The Sun is the ultimate energy source for most food chains, providing the light energy that producers use in photosynthesis.

common_errors.wrong: decomposers are not important to ecosystems
common_errors.correct: Decomposers are essential. Without them, dead matter would accumulate and nutrients would not be recycled back into the soil for producers.

common_errors.wrong: the 10% rule means 10% of organisms survive to the next level
common_errors.correct: The 10% rule means only about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next. The rest is used for life processes and lost as heat.

common_errors.wrong: food chains always start with an animal
common_errors.correct: Food chains almost always start with a producer (plant, algae, or photosynthetic bacteria) that converts solar energy to chemical energy.

common_errors.wrong: bigger animals are always at the top of the food chain
common_errors.correct: Trophic level depends on what an organism eats, not its size. An elephant (herbivore) is at a lower trophic level than a tiny weasel (carnivore).

common_errors.wrong: herbivores are weak because they only eat plants
common_errors.correct: Many herbivores are large and powerful (elephants, rhinos, bison). Diet does not determine physical strength.

facts.statement: A biome is a large region characterized by its climate, plants, and animals
Tropical rainforests have the greatest biodiversity of any terrestrial biome and receive over 200 cm of rain per year
Deserts receive less than 25 cm of precipitation per year; they can be hot (Sahara) or cold (Antarctica)
The tundra is the coldest biome, with permafrost (permanently frozen ground), found in the Arctic and on mountaintops
The taiga (boreal forest) is the world's largest terrestrial biome, dominated by coniferous trees like spruce and pine
Grasslands (prairies, savannas) are dominated by grasses rather than trees and can support large herds of grazing animals
Coral reefs are underwater structures built by colonies of coral polyps and support about 25% of all marine species despite covering less than 1% of the ocean floor
Temperate deciduous forests have four distinct seasons; trees shed leaves in fall to conserve water during winter
Estuaries are areas where freshwater rivers meet saltwater oceans, creating highly productive ecosystems that serve as nurseries for many fish species
Wetlands (marshes, swamps, bogs) act as natural water filters, flood buffers, and carbon sinks, and support high biodiversity
The chaparral (Mediterranean) biome has hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters; plants are adapted to fire and drought
The open ocean (pelagic zone) is the largest biome by area but has relatively low productivity per unit area due to limited nutrients
Alpine biomes occur above the tree line on mountains and share many characteristics with tundra, including cold temperatures and short growing seasons
Savannas are tropical grasslands with scattered trees, found in Africa, South America, and Australia; they have distinct wet and dry seasons
The deep ocean (abyssal zone) is pitch dark, near-freezing, and under extreme pressure, yet supports unique life forms around hydrothermal vents
Mangrove forests grow in coastal saltwater and protect shorelines from erosion, storm surges, and serve as nurseries for fish and crustaceans
Freshwater biomes include lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams; they contain less than 1% of Earth's water but support a high diversity of species

common_errors.wrong: deserts are always hot
common_errors.correct: Deserts are defined by low precipitation, not temperature. Antarctica is technically the largest desert in the world.

common_errors.wrong: the tropical rainforest has the most animals of any ecosystem
common_errors.correct: While tropical rainforests have the greatest terrestrial biodiversity, the ocean as a whole contains more total species.

common_errors.wrong: all forests are the same biome
common_errors.correct: Forest biomes include tropical rainforest, temperate deciduous forest, and taiga/boreal forest, each with very different climates and species.

common_errors.wrong: nothing can live in the deep ocean
common_errors.correct: Deep ocean life includes tube worms, giant squid, anglerfish, and bacteria around hydrothermal vents, thriving without sunlight.

common_errors.wrong: tundra is just a frozen wasteland with no life
common_errors.correct: The tundra supports lichens, mosses, small shrubs, insects, caribou, Arctic foxes, polar bears, and migratory birds during summer.

common_errors.wrong: coral reefs are made of rocks
common_errors.correct: Coral reefs are built by living organisms (coral polyps). The hard structure is calcium carbonate secreted by the polyps over hundreds to thousands of years.

facts.statement: The carbon cycle moves carbon through the atmosphere, organisms, oceans, and rocks via photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, and combustion
Burning fossil fuels releases stored carbon as carbon dioxide, increasing atmospheric CO2 and contributing to climate change
The nitrogen cycle converts atmospheric nitrogen (N2) into usable forms through nitrogen fixation by bacteria, then returns it through denitrification
Most organisms cannot use atmospheric nitrogen (N2) directly; nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil and root nodules convert it to ammonia (NH3)
The phosphorus cycle does not involve the atmosphere; phosphorus moves through rocks, water, soil, and organisms
Carbon sinks include oceans, forests, and soil, which absorb more carbon than they release
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere, but in its N2 form it is unusable by most organisms
Nitrification is the process by which bacteria convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrite (NO2-) and then to nitrate (NO3-), which plants can absorb
Denitrification is the process by which bacteria convert nitrate back to atmospheric nitrogen (N2), completing the nitrogen cycle
The oxygen cycle is tightly linked to the carbon cycle: photosynthesis produces O2, while respiration and combustion consume O2
Oceans absorb about 25-30% of the CO2 humans produce, causing ocean acidification which threatens coral reefs and shellfish
Legumes (beans, peas, clover) have symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules, making them natural soil fertilizers
The global carbon cycle involves fast cycling (photosynthesis/respiration over days to years) and slow cycling (rock formation/volcanism over millions of years)
Excess nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizers cause eutrophication: algal blooms that deplete oxygen and create dead zones in water
The water cycle includes evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff; it is driven by solar energy and gravity
Transpiration is the release of water vapor from plant leaves through stomata; it is a major component of the water cycle
Groundwater is water stored underground in aquifers; it supplies wells and springs and can take thousands of years to replenish

common_errors.wrong: plants only absorb carbon dioxide
common_errors.correct: Plants absorb CO2 for photosynthesis but also release CO2 through cellular respiration. They are net absorbers of CO2.

common_errors.wrong: the nitrogen cycle only involves air and soil
common_errors.correct: The nitrogen cycle involves the atmosphere, soil, water, plants, animals, and bacteria. Lightning can also fix atmospheric nitrogen.

common_errors.wrong: carbon dioxide is the only greenhouse gas
common_errors.correct: Greenhouse gases include CO2, methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), and water vapor. Methane is far more potent per molecule than CO2.

common_errors.wrong: adding more fertilizer always helps plants grow better
common_errors.correct: Excess fertilizer causes water pollution, algal blooms, and dead zones. It can also damage soil microorganisms and change soil pH.

common_errors.wrong: the carbon cycle and climate change are unrelated
common_errors.correct: Climate change is directly caused by disrupting the carbon cycle: burning fossil fuels adds carbon to the atmosphere faster than natural sinks can absorb it.

common_errors.wrong: decomposition only releases carbon dioxide
common_errors.correct: Decomposition releases multiple nutrients including carbon (as CO2), nitrogen (as ammonia), phosphorus, and other minerals back into the soil.

common_errors.wrong: rain comes from the ocean only
common_errors.correct: Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, and plants (transpiration). All of these contribute moisture to the atmosphere for precipitation.

facts.statement: An ecosystem includes all living organisms (biotic factors) and nonliving components (abiotic factors) in an area, interacting as a system
Mutualism is a symbiotic relationship where both species benefit (e.g., bees and flowers)
Parasitism is a relationship where one organism (parasite) benefits at the expense of another (host)
Commensalism is a relationship where one organism benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed
A niche is an organism's role in its ecosystem, including what it eats, where it lives, and how it interacts with other species
Biodiversity refers to the variety of life in an area; higher biodiversity generally makes ecosystems more resilient
Keystone species have a disproportionately large impact on their ecosystem relative to their population size
Invasive species are non-native organisms that spread rapidly and harm native ecosystems by outcompeting native species
Ecological succession is the gradual change in species composition in an area over time: primary succession starts on bare rock, secondary succession follows a disturbance
Carrying capacity is the maximum population size an environment can sustain indefinitely with available resources
Limiting factors (food, water, space, disease) control population size; when resources are scarce, populations decline
The competitive exclusion principle states that two species cannot occupy the exact same niche in the same habitat indefinitely
Abiotic factors include temperature, sunlight, water, soil, wind, and minerals; biotic factors include all living organisms
Pioneer species (lichens, mosses) are the first to colonize bare environments during primary succession, breaking down rock into soil
A climax community is the relatively stable final stage of ecological succession in a given area
Predator-prey relationships help regulate population sizes: as prey increases, predators increase; as predators increase, prey decreases
Mimicry is an adaptation where one species evolves to resemble another: Batesian mimicry (harmless species mimics a dangerous one) and Mullerian mimicry (two harmful species resemble each other)
Camouflage is an adaptation that helps organisms blend into their environment to avoid predators or sneak up on prey

common_errors.wrong: ecosystems and habitats are the same thing
common_errors.correct: A habitat is the physical environment where an organism lives. An ecosystem includes the habitat plus all organisms and their interactions.

common_errors.wrong: competition only occurs between different species
common_errors.correct: Competition occurs both within species (intraspecific) and between species (interspecific).

common_errors.wrong: humans are not part of ecosystems
common_errors.correct: Humans are part of ecosystems and have significant impacts on biodiversity, nutrient cycles, and habitats.

common_errors.wrong: invasive species are always animals
common_errors.correct: Invasive species include plants (kudzu, water hyacinth), animals (cane toads, zebra mussels), fungi, and microorganisms.

common_errors.wrong: an ecosystem can function fine without decomposers
common_errors.correct: Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would be locked away, eventually collapsing the ecosystem.

common_errors.wrong: all symbiotic relationships benefit both organisms
common_errors.correct: Symbiosis means living together closely. It includes mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits), and parasitism (one is harmed).

common_errors.wrong: animals choose to adapt to their environment
common_errors.correct: Adaptations arise through natural selection over many generations. Individual organisms do not choose to develop new traits.

facts.statement: Habitat destruction is the leading cause of species extinction, followed by invasive species, pollution, and overexploitation
Deforestation removes about 10 million hectares of forest per year, releasing stored carbon and destroying habitats
Endangered species are at risk of extinction; the IUCN Red List classifies species from Least Concern to Critically Endangered to Extinct
Acid rain forms when sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels react with water in the atmosphere
Overfishing has depleted many fish populations to levels where they cannot reproduce fast enough to recover
Plastic pollution persists in the environment for hundreds of years; microplastics have been found in oceans, soil, and even in living organisms
Protected areas (national parks, wildlife reserves, marine sanctuaries) help conserve biodiversity by limiting human activity
The current rate of species extinction is estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times higher than the natural background rate
Bioaccumulation is the buildup of toxins in an organism over its lifetime; biomagnification is the increase in toxin concentration at higher trophic levels
Coral bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel their symbiotic algae due to warmer water temperatures, turning white and potentially dying
Sustainable practices aim to meet current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs
Reintroduction programs have helped recover populations of species like the bald eagle, California condor, and gray wolf
The greenhouse effect is a natural process where certain gases in the atmosphere trap heat; human activity has intensified it by adding excess CO2 and methane
The ozone layer in the stratosphere protects life on Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation; it was damaged by CFCs but is recovering due to the Montreal Protocol (1987)
Renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal) produce electricity without burning fossil fuels, reducing greenhouse gas emissions
We should reduce, reuse, and recycle to decrease waste; reducing consumption is the most effective of the three

common_errors.wrong: extinction is a natural process so we don't need to worry about it
common_errors.correct: While extinction is natural, the current rate is 100-1000x the natural rate due to human activity. This rapid loss threatens entire ecosystems.

common_errors.wrong: pollution only affects the area where it is produced
common_errors.correct: Pollution can travel globally through air and water currents. Mercury released in one country can contaminate fish oceans away.

common_errors.wrong: animals can just move to new habitats if theirs is destroyed
common_errors.correct: Many species have specific habitat requirements and cannot survive elsewhere. Habitat fragmentation also creates barriers to movement.

common_errors.wrong: recycling completely solves the waste problem
common_errors.correct: Many materials cannot be infinitely recycled, and recycling itself requires energy. Reducing consumption is more effective than recycling alone.

common_errors.wrong: one person's actions cannot help the environment
common_errors.correct: Individual actions add up: reducing waste, conserving energy, and making sustainable choices collectively have significant impact when practiced by many people.

common_errors.wrong: the greenhouse effect is entirely bad
common_errors.correct: The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life: without it Earth's average temperature would be about -18 degrees C instead of 15 degrees C. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect from human emissions.

common_errors.wrong: the ozone hole and climate change are the same problem
common_errors.correct: The ozone hole (caused by CFCs destroying stratospheric ozone) and climate change (caused by greenhouse gases trapping heat) are separate environmental issues with different causes.

facts.statement: A population is a group of individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time
Population growth rate depends on births, deaths, immigration (moving in), and emigration (moving out)
Exponential growth occurs when a population grows at an ever-increasing rate with unlimited resources, producing a J-shaped curve
Logistic growth occurs when population growth slows as it approaches the carrying capacity, producing an S-shaped curve
Density-dependent limiting factors (disease, competition, predation) have greater effects when populations are crowded
Density-independent limiting factors (natural disasters, weather extremes, pollution) affect populations regardless of their size

r-selected species (bacteria, insects, mice) reproduce rapidly with many offspring and little parental care; K-selected species (elephants, whales, humans) have fewer offspring with more parental investment
The human population has grown from about 1 billion in 1800 to over 8 billion today, largely due to advances in agriculture, medicine, and sanitation
An age structure diagram (population pyramid) shows the distribution of ages in a population and can predict future growth trends
Population density is the number of individuals per unit area; organisms can have clumped, uniform, or random distribution patterns
When a population exceeds its carrying capacity, resources become scarce and the population typically declines until it stabilizes
Endangered species have populations so small that they are at risk of extinction; critically endangered species have fewer than 250 mature individuals

common_errors.wrong: populations always grow continuously
common_errors.correct: Populations cannot grow forever. They are limited by resources, disease, predation, and other factors. Growth slows as carrying capacity is reached.

common_errors.wrong: carrying capacity never changes
common_errors.correct: Carrying capacity can change if environmental conditions change: drought, habitat destruction, or new food sources can raise or lower it.

common_errors.wrong: if we remove predators, prey populations will be healthier
common_errors.correct: Without predators, prey populations often overshoot carrying capacity, overgraze their food supply, and then crash due to starvation and disease.

common_errors.wrong: extinction only affects the species that goes extinct
common_errors.correct: When a species goes extinct, it affects all the organisms that depended on it for food, pollination, seed dispersal, or other ecological roles.

common_errors.wrong: human population growth has always been rapid
common_errors.correct: For most of human history, population grew very slowly. Rapid growth began only in the last 200 years with industrialization, modern agriculture, and medicine.

facts.statement: Natural resources are materials from Earth that living things use; they include air, water, soil, minerals, fossil fuels, plants, and animals
Renewable resources can be replenished naturally over short periods: solar energy, wind, water, and trees (if replanted)
Nonrenewable resources exist in limited supply and take millions of years to form: fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and minerals
Fossil fuels formed from the remains of ancient organisms buried and compressed over millions of years; burning them releases stored carbon as CO2
Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using photovoltaic cells; the Sun provides more energy in one hour than all of humanity uses in a year
Wind turbines convert the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity; wind is caused by uneven heating of Earth's surface by the Sun
Hydroelectric power generates electricity from flowing water, typically by using dams; it is the most widely used renewable energy source globally
Soil is a natural resource that takes hundreds of years to form just a few centimeters; it supports plant growth and stores water and carbon
Fresh water makes up only about 3% of all water on Earth, and most of that is frozen in ice caps and glaciers; less than 1% is readily available for human use
Geothermal energy uses heat from inside the Earth (from radioactive decay and residual heat) to generate electricity or heat buildings
Composting turns food and yard waste into nutrient-rich soil, reducing the amount of waste sent to landfills
Trees are a renewable resource when managed sustainably through replanting; they provide oxygen, absorb CO2, prevent erosion, and support biodiversity
Nuclear energy is a nonrenewable energy source that produces electricity through nuclear fission without direct CO2 emissions, but creates radioactive waste
Biomass energy comes from burning plant material or converting it to biofuels; it is renewable but still releases CO2 when burned
Clean drinking water is one of the most critical natural resources; over 2 billion people worldwide lack access to safely managed drinking water
Topsoil erosion from deforestation, overgrazing, and poor farming practices is a serious environmental problem because soil takes centuries to form
Turning off lights, using energy-efficient appliances, and reducing car trips are simple ways individuals can conserve energy and reduce pollution
Many minerals used in electronics (lithium, cobalt, rare earth elements) are nonrenewable and their mining can cause significant environmental damage
Crop rotation and cover cropping are sustainable farming practices that maintain soil health and reduce the need for synthetic fertilizers
An ecological footprint measures the total area of land and water required to produce the resources a person consumes and absorb the waste they generate

common_errors.wrong: natural resources will never run out
common_errors.correct: Nonrenewable resources like fossil fuels and minerals exist in finite quantities and can be depleted. Even renewable resources can be exhausted if overused (like overfishing).

common_errors.wrong: renewable energy has no environmental impact
common_errors.correct: While cleaner than fossil fuels, renewable energy can still impact the environment: dams alter river ecosystems, wind turbines can affect birds, and solar farms use large areas of land.

common_errors.wrong: we have plenty of fresh water since Earth is covered in water
common_errors.correct: 97% of Earth's water is saltwater. Of the 3% that is freshwater, most is locked in ice. Less than 1% is available for drinking, agriculture, and industry.

common_errors.wrong: soil is just dirt and not important
common_errors.correct: Soil is a complex living ecosystem containing minerals, organic matter, water, air, and billions of organisms. It is essential for growing food and filtering water.

common_errors.wrong: fossil fuels are made from dinosaur bones
common_errors.correct: Fossil fuels formed primarily from ancient marine organisms (plankton, algae) and plants that were buried and compressed over millions of years, not from dinosaur remains.
